before.content_html:
La Vie Scolaire — School Life

This lesson covers Topic 3B of AQA Theme 1: Life at School. You need to describe your school building and facilities, talk about rules and uniform, and give opinions about daily school life. These topics regularly appear in writing tasks (both 90-word and 150-word), listening comprehension, and the photo card discussion in the speaking exam.

Mon Collège — Describing Your School

la bibliothèque — library | Dans mon collège, il y a une grande bibliothèque.
la cantine — canteen | Je mange à la cantine à midi.
la cour de récréation — playground / courtyard | On joue au foot dans la cour.
la salle de classe — classroom | Il n’y a pas beaucoup de salles de classe.
le terrain de sport — sports field | Il y a un terrain de sport derrière le bâtiment.
le gymnase — gym | On fait du sport dans le gymnase.
le laboratoire / le labo — lab | Le labo de sciences est moderne.
le bureau — office / desk | Le bureau du directeur est au premier étage.

When describing your school, use il y a (there is/are), il n’y a pas de (there is no), and on peut (you can / we can) to build detailed sentences. For example:

Mon collège s’appelle Collège Jules Verne. C’est un collège mixte et il y a environ sept cents élèves. Dans mon collège, il y a une grande bibliothèque. Cependant, il n’y a pas de terrain de foot.

Key Fact

After il n’y a pas, the article changes to de/d’ regardless of gender: il y a une piscine but il n’y a pas de piscine. This rule applies whenever a noun follows a negative expression.

Les Règles — School Rules

The specification requires you to discuss rules, permissions and prohibitions. Three key structures are used to express what you must, can, or cannot do at school.

Key Fact

Expressing obligation, permission and prohibition:
Il faut + infinitive = You must / It is necessary to
Il faut arriver à l’heure. (You must arrive on time.)

On doit + infinitive = You/We must
On doit porter un uniforme. (You must wear a uniform.)

Il est interdit de + infinitive = It is forbidden to
Il est interdit de manger en classe. (It is forbidden to eat in class.)

On ne peut pas + infinitive = You cannot / We are not allowed to
On ne peut pas utiliser son portable pendant les leçons.

You can also use these impersonal structures to add variety:
il est nécessaire de — it is necessary to
il est essentiel de — it is essential to
il est important de — it is important to
il est permis de — it is allowed to
il est impossible de — it is impossible to
il est indispensable de — it is vital to
All follow the pattern: il est + adjective + de + infinitive.

L’Uniforme — School Uniform

School uniform is a popular exam topic because it allows you to give opinions for and against, which examiners reward highly. In France, students generally do not wear uniforms — though some schools have recently experimented with reintroducing them.

un pantalon — trousers | une jupe — skirt | une chemise — shirt
un polo — polo shirt | un pull — jumper | une veste — blazer/jacket
une cravate — tie | des chaussures (f) — shoes | des chaussettes (f) — socks
des baskets (f) — trainers | un jean — jeans | un t-shirt — t-shirt
Colours: noir(e) — black | blanc/blanche — white | bleu(e) — blue | gris(e) — grey | rouge — red

Pour (For):
L’uniforme est moins cher que les autres vêtements. — The uniform is cheaper than other clothes.
On ne perd pas de temps à choisir les vêtements le matin. — You don’t waste time choosing clothes in the morning.
L’uniforme nous donne le sentiment d’appartenir à une communauté. — The uniform gives us a sense of belonging to a community.
On est tous habillés de la même façon donc on est moins harcelés. — We are all dressed the same so we are less bullied.

Contre (Against):
L’uniforme n’est pas à la mode. — The uniform is not fashionable.
On ne peut pas montrer sa personnalité. — You can’t show your personality.
L’uniforme n’est pas confortable surtout quand il fait chaud. — The uniform is not comfortable, especially when it is hot.

La Journée Scolaire — The School Day

Describing a typical school day draws together several language skills: telling the time, naming subjects, describing facilities, and using different tenses. Here is a model paragraph.

Dans mon collège, les règles sont assez strictes. Tout d’abord, on doit porter un uniforme. En classe, il est interdit de manger des bonbons et on doit toujours lever la main pour parler. Si on arrive en retard, on se fait crier dessus. Cependant, on peut utiliser son téléphone portable dans la cour, ce qui est bien.

Translation: In my school, the rules are quite strict. First of all, you must wear a uniform. In class, it is forbidden to eat sweets and you must always put your hand up to speak. If you arrive late, you get told off. However, you can use your mobile phone in the yard, which is good.

Key Fact

In French, la laïcité (secularism) means that religious symbols are banned in French state schools. This is a useful cultural point to mention in the speaking exam when discussing differences between French and English schools.

Les Amis — Talking About Friends

Friendships are a key topic in AQA GCSE French, falling under Theme 1: People and Lifestyle. The exam tests your ability to describe your friends, explain what makes a good friend, give opinions about friendship, and use different tenses when talking about relationships. This lesson covers the essential vocabulary, opinion phrases and the near future tense (le futur proche).

Essential friendship vocabulary from the AQA prescribed list:

  • un(e) ami(e) — a friend | un copain / une copine — a mate/friend
  • le/la meilleur(e) ami(e) — best friend
  • s’entendre (bien/mal) avec — to get on (well/badly) with
  • se disputer avec — to argue with
  • passer du temps avec — to spend time with
  • se ressembler — to be alike / to resemble each other
  • la confiance — trust | le soutien — support
  • le respect — respect | la qualité — quality

What Makes a Good Friend?

A common exam task asks you to describe the qualities of a good friend. The key structure is: Un bon ami doit être... (A good friend must be...) followed by adjectives. You can also use Il faut... (It is necessary to...) to explain what friendship requires.

Key Fact

Key qualities: Un bon ami doit être fidèle (loyal), honnête (honest), gentil (kind), patient (patient) and drôle (funny). A good friend doit écouter (must listen), encourager (encourage) and soutenir (support) you.

You can extend your answers using opinion phrases:

  • À mon avis — In my opinion
  • Je pense que — I think that | Je trouve que — I find that
  • Je crois que — I believe that | Personnellement — Personally
  • Ce que j’aime le plus — What I like the most

Use these graduated opinion verbs to express how you feel about your friends and friendship:

  • J’adore (I love) → J’aime (I like) → Je n’aime pas (I don’t like) → Je déteste (I hate)
  • Je préfère (I prefer) | Ça me plaît (It pleases me) | Ça m’énerve (It annoys me)
  • J’en ai marre de (I’m fed up with) | Je ne peux pas supporter (I can’t stand)

Example: À mon avis, la chose la plus importante dans l’amitié, c’est la confiance. Je ne peux pas supporter les gens qui mentent. (In my opinion, the most important thing in friendship is trust. I can’t stand people who lie.)

Le Futur Proche — The Near Future Tense

The near future tense is one of the easiest tenses to form in French. It lets you talk about what you are going to do. The AQA exam rewards using multiple tenses, so adding the near future to your writing and speaking is a straightforward way to access higher marks.

Key Fact

To form the near future: use the present tense of aller (to go) + the infinitive of the main verb. For example: Je vais sortir avec mes amis ce week-end (I am going to go out with my friends this weekend).

The verb aller is irregular in the present tense:

  • je vais (I go) | tu vas (you go) | il/elle/on va (he/she/one goes)
  • nous allons (we go) | vous allez (you go, formal/pl) | ils/elles vont (they go)

Near future examples with friendship vocabulary:

  • Je vais passer du temps avec mon meilleur ami. — I am going to spend time with my best friend.
  • Nous allons aller au cinéma ensemble. — We are going to go to the cinema together.
  • Elle va rencontrer ses copines samedi. — She is going to meet her friends on Saturday.

Describing Your Best Friend — Model Answer

Here is a model paragraph that combines friendship vocabulary, opinions and the near future tense:

Mon meilleur ami s’appelle Thomas. Je m’entends très bien avec lui car il est fidèle et honnête. On se ressemble beaucoup — nous aimons tous les deux le football et les jeux vidéo. À mon avis, la chose la plus importante dans l’amitié, c’est la confiance. Parfois on se dispute, mais on se réconcilie toujours. Ce week-end, nous allons jouer au foot ensemble.

This paragraph uses: present tense (s’appelle, m’entends, se ressemble, aimons, se dispute), an opinion phrase (à mon avis), the relative pronoun car (because), and the near future tense (nous allons jouer). Using three tenses or time frames in your writing is key to reaching the higher levels.

Key Fact

The AQA mark scheme rewards the use of three time frames (past, present, future) in writing and speaking tasks. The near future tense is the easiest way to add a future time frame to your answer.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Learn common occupations in both masculine and feminine forms — examiners check for accurate gender agreement in job titles.
  • The conditional tense is formed with the infinitive (or irregular stem) + imperfect endings. Key forms: je voudrais, j’aimerais, je serais, je ferais.
  • Combine three future structures in your writing — near future (je vais), conditional (je voudrais), and simple future (je travaillerai) — to demonstrate range and score highly.

before.content_html:
Technology in Daily Life

Technology and social media are popular exam topics in AQA GCSE French. You need to describe how you use technology, give opinions on its advantages and disadvantages, and discuss screen time and online safety. This topic often appears in the writing and speaking exams.

un portable — a mobile phone / laptop. J’utilise mon portable tous les jours.

un ordinateur — a computer. J’ai un ordinateur dans ma chambre.

une tablette — a tablet. Ma sœur préfère utiliser sa tablette.

les réseaux sociaux — social media / social networks. Je passe trop de temps sur les réseaux sociaux.

un site web — a website. J’ai créé un site web pour mon projet.

télécharger — to download. Je télécharge de la musique et des applications.

envoyer des messages / des textos — to send messages / texts. J’envoie des textos à mes amis.

Key Fact

The word portable can mean either a mobile phone or a laptop in French, depending on context. Mon portable usually means “my phone” in everyday conversation, but un ordinateur portable specifically means “a laptop.”

What You Do Online

You should be able to describe your online activities in detail:

faire des recherches (to do research), regarder des vidéos (to watch videos), jouer à des jeux en ligne (to play online games), écouter de la musique (to listen to music), tchatter avec mes amis (to chat with my friends), poster des photos (to post photos), lire des articles (to read articles).

Advantages & Disadvantages of Technology

Giving a balanced argument about technology is a key skill for the writing and speaking exams. Use the structure d’un côté … de l’autre côté (on one hand … on the other hand) to present both sides.

On peut communiquer facilement avec des gens partout dans le monde. — You can communicate easily with people all over the world.

C’est utile pour faire des recherches pour les devoirs. — It’s useful for doing homework research.

On peut rester en contact avec sa famille et ses amis. — You can stay in touch with family and friends.

C’est un bon moyen de se divertir. — It’s a good way to have fun / entertain yourself.

On passe trop de temps devant l’écran. — You spend too much time in front of the screen.

Le cyberharcèlement est un problème grave. — Cyberbullying is a serious problem.

C’est mauvais pour la santé — on ne fait pas assez d’exercice. — It’s bad for health — you don’t do enough exercise.

Il y a un risque de dépendance. — There is a risk of addiction.

Using pour and afin de

The structures pour (in order to) and afin de (in order to) are followed by an infinitive and are excellent for adding purpose to your sentences:

J’utilise mon portable pour envoyer des messages. (I use my phone to send messages.)

Je vais sur Internet afin de faire des recherches. (I go on the Internet in order to do research.)

J’utilise les réseaux sociaux pour rester en contact avec mes amis. (I use social media to stay in touch with my friends.)

Key Fact

Using afin de instead of pour shows the examiner you can vary your language. Both mean “in order to” and are followed by an infinitive. Other useful purpose structures include: dans le but de (with the aim of) and pour que + subjunctive (so that).

Opinions About Technology

Strong opinion phrases to use in the exam:

À mon avis (in my opinion), je pense que (I think that), je crois que (I believe that), selon moi (according to me), il me semble que (it seems to me that), je suis convaincu(e) que (I am convinced that).

Example: À mon avis, la technologie est très utile pour les études, mais il faut limiter le temps d’écran afin de protéger sa santé.

La Nourriture et les Boissons — Food and Drink

Food and drink vocabulary is tested across all four AQA exam papers. You need to be able to name common foods, describe meals, order in a restaurant, and give opinions about what you eat and drink. This lesson covers the essential vocabulary, partitive articles (du, de la, des), and how to talk about mealtimes.

Essential food vocabulary from the AQA prescribed list:

  • le pain — bread | le fromage — cheese | le lait — milk
  • le poisson — fish | le poulet — chicken | la viande — meat
  • les fruits — fruit | les légumes — vegetables | les légumes frais — fresh vegetables
  • le gâteau — cake | la glace — ice cream | les frites — chips/fries
  • le plat — dish/course | la recette — recipe | la carte — menu
  • le goût — taste | la nourriture — food | la cuisine — cooking/kitchen

Essential drink vocabulary:

  • l’eau (f) — water | le thé — tea | le café — coffee
  • le jus d’orange — orange juice | la boisson — drink | le lait — milk

Les Articles Partitifs — Partitive Articles

When talking about food and drink in French, you must use the correct partitive articles. These are used to say “some” and are essential for food vocabulary. In English, we often leave out “some” (“I eat bread”), but in French you must always include the partitive article (“Je mange du pain”).

Key Fact

The partitive articles are: du (before masculine nouns — du pain, du fromage), de la (before feminine nouns — de la viande, de la glace), de l’ (before vowels — de l’eau), and des (before plural nouns — des fruits, des légumes).

Important rule: After a negative, the partitive article changes to de (or d’ before a vowel). For example: Je mange du poisson (I eat fish) → Je ne mange pas de poisson (I don’t eat fish). This is a very common exam question.

Positive sentences:

  • Je mange du pain et du fromage. — I eat (some) bread and cheese.
  • Elle boit de l’eau. — She drinks (some) water.
  • Nous mangeons des légumes frais. — We eat (some) fresh vegetables.
  • Il prend de la glace. — He has (some) ice cream.

Negative sentences (partitive becomes de/d’):

  • Je ne mange pas de viande. — I don’t eat (any) meat.
  • Il ne boit pas d’alcool. — He doesn’t drink (any) alcohol.

Les Repas — Mealtimes

In France, there are three main meals. Knowing how to talk about each one is important for writing and speaking tasks about daily routine and healthy eating.

Key Fact

The three meals: le petit déjeuner (breakfast), le déjeuner (lunch), and le dîner (dinner/evening meal). Use the structure Au petit déjeuner, je mange... (For breakfast, I eat...) or Au déjeuner, je prends... (For lunch, I have...).

From the source material, here is a model description of meals:

Mon régime comprend des fruits, des légumes frais, du poisson, du poulet, du pain, du lait et du fromage. Au petit déjeuner, je mange un repas léger. Au déjeuner, je prends un bon plat chaud. Au dîner, je mange une soupe avant d’aller au lit. Après le repas, je bois de l’eau, du thé ou du café, et parfois je prends une glace.

This paragraph uses partitive articles correctly throughout, names all three meals, and includes a variety of food vocabulary. It would score well in a writing task about diet and healthy living.

Giving Opinions About Food

Adding opinions to your food descriptions shows the examiner you can express personal views, which is key to accessing higher marks. Use the connectives you already know to build longer, more complex sentences.

  • J’adore le chocolat car c’est délicieux. — I love chocolate because it is delicious.
  • Je déteste les légumes parce que je trouve que c’est fade. — I hate vegetables because I find them bland.
  • Mon plat préféré, c’est le poulet rôti. — My favourite dish is roast chicken.
  • Je suis végétarien(ne), donc je ne mange pas de viande. — I am vegetarian, so I don’t eat meat.
Key Fact

Certains deviennent végétariens pour améliorer leur régime ou pour des raisons éthiques. — Some become vegetarian to improve their diet or for ethical reasons. This is a higher-level phrase from the source material that shows sophisticated language use. The words végétarien and végan are on the AQA prescribed vocabulary list.

When writing about food, try to combine description, opinion and explanation in each sentence. For example: Au petit déjeuner, je mange des céréales et je bois du jus d’orange parce que c’est sain et énergique (For breakfast, I eat cereal and drink orange juice because it is healthy and energising). This shows the examiner three things at once: vocabulary range, opinion, and a connective.

Les Relations — Relationships

This lesson covers relationships, marriage and future plans — a topic that appears regularly in AQA GCSE French writing and speaking tasks. You need to be able to discuss different types of relationships, give your opinion on marriage, and talk about your future plans using the conditional tense.

Essential vocabulary from the AQA prescribed list:

  • le couple — couple | le/la partenaire — partner
  • le mariage — marriage/wedding | se marier — to get married
  • le PACS — civil partnership | se séparer — to separate
  • célibataire — single | ensemble — together
  • l’amour — love | le sentiment — feeling
  • sortir avec — to go out with | tomber amoureux/amoureuse (de) — to fall in love (with)
  • le mariage du même sexe — same-sex marriage
  • l’indépendance — independence | la tradition — tradition

Opinions on Marriage

The exam often asks you to discuss the pros and cons of marriage. Being able to argue both sides shows the examiner you can construct a balanced response, which is key for higher-level writing tasks.

Arguments in favour of marriage:

  • Le mariage montre un engagement sérieux. — Marriage shows a serious commitment.
  • C’est une tradition importante dans beaucoup de cultures. — It is an important tradition in many cultures.
  • Le mariage donne une sécurité légale au couple. — Marriage gives legal security to the couple.
  • C’est une belle célébration de l’amour. — It is a beautiful celebration of love.

Arguments against marriage:

  • Ce n’est pas nécessaire — on peut être heureux sans se marier. — It is not necessary — you can be happy without getting married.
  • Le mariage coûte très cher. — Marriage costs a lot of money.
  • Beaucoup de mariages finissent par un divorce. — Many marriages end in divorce.
  • On peut choisir un PACS, qui est plus simple. — You can choose a PACS (civil partnership), which is simpler.
Key Fact

The PACS (Pacte Civil de Solidarité) is a French civil partnership available to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples. It gives many of the same legal rights as marriage but is simpler and cheaper to arrange. Since 2013, same-sex marriage (le mariage pour tous) has been legal in France.

Le Conditionnel — The Conditional Tense

The conditional tense is used to say what you would do. It is essential for talking about future plans, wishes and hypothetical situations. At Foundation level, you only need the singular forms of a few key verbs. At Higher level, you should be able to use it more broadly.

Key Fact

To form the conditional: take the infinitive of the verb (the future stem) and add the imperfect endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. For example: aimer → j’aimerais (I would like), habiter → j’habiterais (I would live).

The most useful conditional forms for this topic:

  • j’aimerais — I would like | je voudrais — I would like/want (irregular: vouloir → voudr-)
  • je serais — I would be (irregular: être → ser-) | j’aurais — I would have (irregular: avoir → aur-)
  • j’habiterais — I would live | je travaillerais — I would work
  • ce serait — it would be | j’irais — I would go (irregular: aller → ir-)

Irregular stems to learn: avoir → aur-, être → ser-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, vouloir → voudr-, pouvoir → pourr-

Talking About Future Plans

The exam frequently asks about your future plans for relationships and family. Use these structures to talk about what you would like in the future:

  • Quand je serai plus âgé(e), j’aimerais... — When I am older, I would like...
  • À l’avenir, je voudrais... — In the future, I would like...
  • Je ne vais pas me marier car je pense que ce n’est pas nécessaire. — I am not going to get married because I think it is not necessary.
Key Fact

Example model answer: À l’avenir, je voudrais me marier et avoir deux enfants. J’aimerais que mon partenaire soit gentil et honnête. Ce serait idéal d’habiter à la campagne. (In the future, I would like to get married and have two children. I would like my partner to be kind and honest. It would be ideal to live in the countryside.)

Notice how the model answer uses the conditional (voudrais, aimerais, serait) alongside opinion structures. This combination of tenses and opinions is exactly what the examiner rewards at the higher levels of the mark scheme.

La musique, le cinéma et la télévision

Entertainment is a core topic in AQA GCSE French Theme 2. You need to describe what music, films and TV programmes you enjoy, give opinions with reasons, and talk about entertainment experiences in the past. This lesson covers the key vocabulary, opinion phrases, adjective agreement, and the perfect tense with être.

Key Fact

the specification lists entertainment vocabulary under “Free-time activities.” In the exam, you could be asked to describe a film you have seen, a concert you attended, or your favourite TV programme in any of the four skills.

Key Vocabulary: Music

un chanteur / une chanteuse — a singer. Mon chanteur préféré est très talentueux. (My favourite singer is very talented.)

un groupe — a band. Ce groupe fait de la musique pop. (This band makes pop music.)

une chanson — a song. J’adore cette chanson car elle est énergique. (I love this song because it’s energetic.)

écouter de la musique — to listen to music. J’écoute de la musique tous les jours. (I listen to music every day.)

un concert — a concert. Je suis allé(e) à un concert l’année dernière. (I went to a concert last year.)

télécharger — to download. Je télécharge de la musique sur mon portable. (I download music on my phone.)

Key Vocabulary: Film & Television

un film d’action / une comédie / un film d’horreur / un dessin animé — an action film / a comedy / a horror film / a cartoon. Je préfère les comédies car elles sont drôles.

un acteur / une actrice — an actor / an actress. Cet acteur est très connu en France. (This actor is very well-known in France.)

regarder la télé — to watch TV. Le soir, je regarde la télé avec ma famille. (In the evening, I watch TV with my family.)

une émission — a programme / show. Mon émission préférée est une série policière. (My favourite programme is a crime series.)

une série — a series / TV show. Je regarde des séries en streaming. (I watch series on streaming.)

aller au cinéma — to go to the cinema. Je suis allé(e) au cinéma samedi dernier. (I went to the cinema last Saturday.)

Grammar Focus: Adjective Agreement

In French, adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in gender and number. This is especially important when giving opinions about entertainment.

The basic rules: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural. Some adjectives are irregular: bon → bonne, beau → belle, nouveau → nouvelle, vieux → vieille. Adjectives ending in -eux change to -euse in the feminine: ennuyeux → ennuyeuse.

Key Fact

Adjective agreement errors are penalised in the Writing exam as minor errors. However, if the error changes meaning or shows a lack of grammatical understanding, it can be treated as a major error. Always check the gender of the noun before writing the adjective.

Grammar Focus: Perfect Tense with être

Most verbs form the perfect tense with avoir, but a group of verbs of movement use être instead. When using être, the past participle must agree with the subject.

The key être verbs to learn (remembered by the mnemonic MRS VAN DER TRAMP): monter, rester, sortir, venir, aller, naître, descendre, entrer, retourner, tomber, rentrer, arriver, mourir, partir.

Agreement rules: add -e to the past participle for a feminine subject, -s for a masculine plural subject, -es for a feminine plural subject. For example: Il est allé (he went), Elle est allée (she went), Ils sont allés (they went, masc.), Elles sont allées (they went, fem.).

Je suis allé(e) au cinéma. — I went to the cinema.

Elle est sortie avec ses amies. — She went out with her friends.

Nous sommes arrivés en retard au concert. — We arrived late at the concert.

Ils sont venus chez moi pour regarder un film. — They came to my house to watch a film.

Ma sœur est restée à la maison pour regarder la télé. — My sister stayed at home to watch TV.

Key Fact

Forgetting past participle agreement with être verbs is one of the most common mistakes in the Writing exam. If you are female or writing about a female, always add the -e.

La Famille — Family Members

Being able to talk about your family is one of the most important topics in GCSE French. The AQA exam expects you to describe your family members, say who they are, and give opinions about your relationships with them. You will need this vocabulary across all four papers — listening, speaking, reading and writing.

Here are the essential family members you must know for the exam:

  • le père — father | la mère — mother
  • le frère — brother | la sœur — sister
  • le grand-père — grandfather | la grand-mère — grandmother
  • l’oncle — uncle | la tante — aunt
  • le cousin / la cousine — cousin
  • le fils — son | la fille — daughter
  • le beau-père — stepfather | la belle-mère — stepmother
  • le mari — husband | la femme — wife
Key Fact

In French, every noun has a gender — masculine (le) or feminine (la). Family members often come in pairs: le frère (brother) and la sœur (sister). Learning both forms together helps you remember the genders.

Les Adjectifs Possessifs — Possessive Adjectives

In French, possessive adjectives agree with the noun they describe, not with the person who owns the thing. This is different from English. For example, “his sister” and “her sister” are both sa sœur because sœur is feminine.

The possessive adjectives change depending on whether the noun is masculine, feminine or plural:

  • My: mon (m) / ma (f) / mes (pl) — mon père, ma mère, mes parents
  • Your (tu): ton (m) / ta (f) / tes (pl) — ton frère, ta sœur, tes cousins
  • His/Her: son (m) / sa (f) / ses (pl) — son oncle, sa tante, ses grands-parents

Important exception: Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, use mon/ton/son instead of ma/ta/sa for pronunciation. For example: mon amie (my friend, female), not ma amie.

Describing Physical Appearance

To describe someone’s physical appearance in French, you use two key structures. For hair, use avoir (to have): J’ai les cheveux blonds (I have blond hair). For eyes, also use avoir: Il a les yeux bleus (He has blue eyes). For height and build, use être (to be): Elle est grande et mince (She is tall and slim).

Key Fact

In French, adjectives must agree in gender and number with the noun they describe. A boy is petit but a girl is petite. Boys are petits and girls are petites. This adjectival agreement is tested in every writing and translation task.

Hair: les cheveux longs (long), courts (short), blonds (blond), bruns (brown), noirs (black), roux (red/ginger).

Eyes: les yeux bleus (blue), verts (green), marron (brown — note: marron never changes form).

Build: grand(e) (tall), petit(e) (short), mince (slim), fort(e) (strong/stocky).

Other: Il/Elle porte des lunettes (He/She wears glasses), Il/Elle a une barbe (He/She has a beard).

Describing Personality

Personality descriptions use être (to be) followed by an adjective. Here are the key adjectives from the AQA prescribed vocabulary list:

  • Positive: sympa/sympathique (nice), gentil(le) (kind), amusant(e) (funny), intelligent(e) (clever), sérieux/sérieuse (serious/hardworking), drôle (funny)
  • Negative: méchant(e) (mean/nasty), paresseux/paresseuse (lazy), timide (shy), ennuyeux/ennuyeuse (boring), embêtant(e) (annoying), bavard(e) (chatty)

Putting It All Together

In the exam, you need to combine family vocabulary, possessive adjectives and descriptions into full sentences. Here is a model paragraph:

Key Fact

J’ai une grande famille. Mon père s’appelle Marc. Il a les cheveux courts et bruns. Il est grand et sympa. Ma mère est petite et très gentille. J’ai un frère qui s’appelle Mathieu — il est amusant mais parfois paresseux.

Notice how the paragraph uses avoir for hair and family members, être for personality and build, possessive adjectives (mon, ma), and the relative pronoun qui to add extra detail. These are exactly the structures the examiner is looking for.

La Santé — Healthy Living

Healthy living and lifestyle is a major topic in AQA GCSE French, forming Topic 2 of Theme 1 (People and Lifestyle). The exam expects you to discuss health, fitness, diet, and the dangers of unhealthy habits. You need vocabulary for food and exercise, structures using il faut + infinitive, and reflexive verbs for daily routines.

Essential health vocabulary from the AQA prescribed list:

  • la santé — health | en bonne santé — in good health | en forme — fit/in shape
  • sain(e) — healthy | équilibré(e) — balanced | malade — ill
  • le sport — sport | l’exercice — exercise | l’activité physique — physical activity
  • courir — to run | nager — to swim | marcher — to walk
  • dangereux/dangereuse — dangerous | le tabac — tobacco | la drogue — drugs
  • fumer — to smoke | vapoter — to vape | l’alcool — alcohol
  • la maladie — illness | le stress — stress | fatigué(e) — tired

Il Faut / Il Ne Faut Pas — Giving Advice

The structure il faut + infinitive is one of the most useful in GCSE French. It means “it is necessary to” or “you must” and is used to give advice about health. Its negative form, il ne faut pas, means “you must not”.

Key Fact

Key health advice using il faut: Pour être en bonne santé, il faut bien manger et bien dormir (To be in good health, you must eat well and sleep well). Il faut faire du sport régulièrement (You must do sport regularly). Il ne faut pas fumer (You must not smoke).

You can also use il est important de (it is important to) and il est nécessaire de (it is necessary to) as alternatives to il faut. Using variety in your language structures impresses the examiner.

Il faut... (You must...)

  • bien manger — eat well | bien dormir — sleep well
  • faire du sport — do sport | boire de l’eau — drink water
  • manger sainement — eat healthily | se coucher tôt — go to bed early
  • se laver régulièrement — wash regularly | se détendre — relax

Il ne faut pas... (You must not...)

  • fumer des cigarettes — smoke cigarettes | vapoter — vape
  • boire de l’alcool — drink alcohol | manger trop de fast-food — eat too much fast food

Les Verbes Réflexifs — Reflexive Verbs

Reflexive verbs are essential for describing daily routines and healthy habits. In a reflexive verb, the subject does the action to themselves. They always have an extra pronoun before the verb.

Key Fact

The reflexive pronouns are: me (myself), te (yourself), se (himself/herself/oneself), nous (ourselves), vous (yourselves), se (themselves). Example: Je me couche à dix heures (I go to bed at ten o’clock).

Key reflexive verbs for the health topic:

  • se lever — to get up | Je me lève à sept heures. (I get up at seven.)
  • se coucher — to go to bed | Il se couche tôt. (He goes to bed early.)
  • se laver — to wash (oneself) | Elle se lave tous les matins. (She washes every morning.)
  • se détendre / se relaxer — to relax | Nous nous détendons après le sport. (We relax after sport.)
  • se reposer — to rest | Après un gros effort, il faut se reposer. (After a big effort, you must rest.)
  • se sentir — to feel | Je me sens fatigué. (I feel tired.)

The Dangers of Unhealthy Habits

The AQA exam often includes reading and listening texts about the dangers of smoking, drugs and alcohol. Here are the key phrases from the source material:

  • Le tabac, l’alcool et la drogue sont dangereux pour le corps. — Tobacco, alcohol and drugs are dangerous for the body.
  • Fumer des cigarettes peut causer une maladie ou même la mort. — Smoking cigarettes can cause illness or even death.
  • Une mauvaise alimentation peut causer un manque d’énergie. — A bad diet can cause a lack of energy.
  • Les experts en santé conseillent de prévenir les maladies. — Health experts advise preventing illnesses.

De nos jours, beaucoup de jeunes essaient de mener une vie saine et équilibrée. Pour être en bonne santé, il faut bien manger, bien dormir et faire du sport régulièrement. Je me lève à sept heures et je me couche à dix heures. Le fast-food et l’alcool sont dangereux pour le corps. À mon avis, il est important de prendre soin de soi-même.

This model uses: il faut + infinitive, reflexive verbs (se lever, se coucher), opinion phrases (à mon avis), and topic-specific vocabulary. It would score well for both content and quality of language.

Key Fact

En résumé, il faut prévenir plutôt que guérir — In summary, it is necessary to prevent rather than cure. This is a key phrase from the source material that summarises the French attitude to health. Using it in your writing shows cultural awareness and sophisticated vocabulary.

Booking a Hotel Room

In the AQA GCSE French exam, you may need to understand or produce language about booking accommodation and dealing with problems. This lesson covers the key vocabulary and phrases for hotel role-plays, reading tasks, and writing tasks.

When booking a room, you need to specify: the type of room, the length of stay, any facilities you want, and sometimes meals.

une chambre double — a double room. Je voudrais réserver une chambre double.

une chambre individuelle — a single room. Je souhaite réserver une chambre individuelle avec douche.

une chambre familiale — a family room. Avez-vous une chambre familiale pour quatre personnes?

pour … nuits — for … nights. Pour trois nuits, s’il vous plaît.

pour une semaine / quinze jours — for a week / a fortnight. Nous allons rester pour une semaine.

avec douche / avec bain — with shower / with bath. Je voudrais une chambre avec douche et balcon.

avec vue sur la mer — with a sea view. Est-ce que la chambre a une vue sur la mer?

Key Fact

Three ways to say “I would like” in French: je voudrais (I would like), j’aimerais (I would like/love), je souhaite (I wish to). Using je voudrais or j’aimerais shows you can use the conditional tense — this impresses examiners.

Types of Accommodation

You should know a range of accommodation types:

un hôtel (a hotel), un camping (a campsite), une auberge de jeunesse (a youth hostel), un gîte (a holiday cottage), une chambre d’hôte (a B&B), un appartement (an apartment), une tente (a tent), une caravane (a caravan), une villa (a villa), un château (a castle).

une piscine (chauffée) — a (heated) swimming pool. L’hôtel a une piscine chauffée.

un restaurant / un bar — a restaurant / a bar. Il y a un restaurant et un bar dans l’hôtel.

un parking — a car park. Est-ce qu’il y a un parking?

un ascenseur — a lift. L’ascenseur est en panne.

le wifi (gratuit) — (free) wifi. Il y a du wifi gratuit dans les chambres.

la climatisation — air conditioning. La climatisation ne marche pas.

Meal Plans

You may also need to describe what type of meal plan is included:

le petit-déjeuner compris (breakfast included), en demi-pension (half board — breakfast and dinner), en pension complète (full board — all meals), tout compris (all-inclusive).

Problems & Complaints

A key topic for the speaking and writing exams is dealing with hotel problems. Learn these common phrases for complaints:

Je veux me plaindre — I want to complain. Je veux me plaindre de ma chambre.

… ne marche pas / ne fonctionne pas — … doesn’t work. La douche ne marche pas.

c’est cassé — it’s broken. La télévision est cassée.

la chambre est sale — the room is dirty. La chambre est très sale et petite.

il fait trop chaud / trop froid — it’s too hot / too cold. Il fait trop froid dans la chambre.

il n’y a pas de … — there is no … Il n’y a pas de serviettes.

il y a trop de bruit — there is too much noise. Il y a trop de bruit le soir.

l’ascenseur est en panne — the lift is out of order. L’ascenseur est en panne depuis hier.

Key Fact

When writing a complaint letter or describing a bad hotel experience, use the imperfect tense for descriptions (la chambre était sale — the room was dirty) and the perfect tense for events (j’ai vu une mouche — I saw a fly). Mixing tenses correctly shows the examiner you have strong grammar skills.

Useful phrases for asking for solutions: Y a-t-il une solution? (Is there a solution?), Je voudrais une autre chambre. (I would like another room.), Je voudrais un remboursement. (I would like a refund.)
